title: Review: Experimental design and variables; Statistics: descriptive and spread; Statistical tests; Factors affecting enzyme activity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR02a#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR03b#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ02#N.3a, PR01a#N.6, PR01b#N.12, PR02a#N.11, PR02b#N.7a, PR03a#N.3, PR03b#N.9, EZ02#N.8a, PR01a#N.10, PR01b#N.5, PR02a#N.14, PR03a#N.11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Median
items.clue: The middle value when the values are placed in order.

items.label: Degrees of freedom
items.clue: For comparing two means: the two sample sizes added together, minus 2.

items.label: Random error
items.clue: Unpredictable scatter in readings; repeats and a mean reduce its effect.

items.label: Systematic error
items.clue: Shifts every reading the same way; removed by calibrating, not by repeats.

questions.stem: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³ (illustrative data). What is the best estimate of the initial rate of reaction from these data?

options.text: 0.4 cm³ s⁻¹
20 seconds
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹. With readings every 20 s, this first-interval rate is the best estimate the data allow.

questions.stem: A student plans to test whether the number of double bonds in a fatty acid affects its melting point, using fatty acids with 0, 1, 2 and 3 double bonds that all have the same chain length. Which statement is an appropriate null hypothesis for this investigation?

options.text: Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at lower temperatures than those with fewer.
Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at higher temperatures than those with fewer.
The number of double bonds in a fatty acid has no effect on its melting point.
None of the fatty acids will melt at any of the temperatures used in the investigation.

questions.stem: A student uses a water bath to keep enzyme tubes at 30 °C. Her thermometer gives readings that agree closely: 30.0, 30.0, 30.5, 30.0 °C. A calibrated electronic probe in the same water bath reads 28.0 °C. Which improvement would make her temperature measurements more accurate?

options.text: Take ten readings with the same thermometer and use their mean.
Calibrate the thermometer against the probe, or use the probe instead.
Record each reading to two decimal places, so that the mean is more exact.
Calculate the range of her readings, to show that they are accurate.

questions.explanation: The readings are precise but about 2 °C high: a systematic error. Only calibration (or a calibrated instrument) brings the readings close to the true value.

questions.stem: In a country, the number of new COVID-19 cases recorded per day fell from 2000 in one week to 1600 in the following week. What is the percentage change in the daily number of cases?

options.text: Fell by 25%
Fell by 22%
Fell by 80%
Fell by 20%

questions.explanation: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (1600 − 2000) ÷ 2000 × 100 = −20%, a fall of 20%.

questions.stem: A student grew bean seedlings with fertiliser X or fertiliser Y, 10 plants each. Mean root length ± 1 standard deviation: X, 42 mm (bar from 33 to 51 mm); Y, 47 mm (bar from 39 to 55 mm). Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Fertiliser Y gave significantly longer roots, because its mean is 5 mm higher.
Every root grown with fertiliser X was between 33 and 51 mm long.
The SD bars overlap widely, so the difference may be due to chance alone.
The SD bars overlap, which proves that the two fertilisers have exactly the same effect.

questions.explanation: Most of each bar lies within the other. Many plants in the two groups had similar roots. A t-test, using sample size, would decide whether 5 mm is significant.

questions.stem: A student measures the lengths of 20 leaves from plants growing in the sun and 20 from plants growing in the shade. She wants to know whether mean leaf length differs between the two. Which statistical test should she use?

options.text: Chi-squared, because she is comparing two groups of plants.
Student's t-test, because she is comparing the means of two sets of continuous data.
A correlation coefficient, because she wants to know whether light is related to leaf length.
No test is needed: if the two means differ, the difference is real.

questions.explanation: Two groups, one measured variable, a difference in means: that is what the t-test is for.

questions.stem: A student counts the heart rate of Daphnia in pond water (control) and in a caffeine solution, 10 Daphnia in each. - Control: mean 212 beats per minute, SD 18. - Caffeine: mean 231 beats per minute, SD 20. Critical values of t at p = 0.05: 9 degrees of freedom, 2.26; 18, 2.10; 20, 2.09. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: t = 9.75, far above 2.10, so the difference is highly significant.
t = 2.23, above 2.10 for 18 degrees of freedom, so reject the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, below 2.26 for 9 degrees of freedom, so accept the null hypothesis.
t = 2.23, above 2.10, which proves caffeine raises the heart rate of every Daphnia.

questions.stem: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. When it passes with food into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity falls almost to zero. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The change in pH alters charges on amino acids, disrupting bonds that hold the active site's shape.
The alkaline conditions hydrolyse the peptide bonds of pepsin, breaking it up into free amino acids.
Pepsin has run out of substrate, because protein digestion is completed inside the stomach.
At pH 8 the enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly, so they collide less often.

questions.stem: Ecologists want to test the hypothesis that two limpet species compete for algae on a shore. Which approach tests the hypothesis by experiment rather than by observation?

options.text: Removing one limpet species from marked plots and recording the growth of the other over a year.
Recording the abundance of both limpet species in quadrats placed at random positions along the shore.
Measuring the shell sizes of both limpet species in laboratory tanks of seawater collected from the shore.
Applying a chi-squared test to records of where each species occurred in past shore surveys.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder's mass falls from 3.62 g to 3.40 g in a sucrose solution. The balance reads to ±0.01 g. What is the percentage error in the change in mass?
questions.explanation: Change = 3.62 − 3.40 = 0.22 g, uncertainty = 0.01 + 0.01 = ±0.02 g (OCR form: 2 × 0.01). Percentage error = 0.02 ÷ 0.22 × 100 = 9.1%. A small change carries a large percentage error.

questions.stem: The lengths of five seedling roots, in mm, are 14, 16, 15, 18 and 17. Which gives the mean and standard deviation correctly?

options.text: Mean 16 mm; SD 1.4 mm.
Mean 16 mm; SD 2.5 mm.
Mean 16 mm; SD 1.6 mm.
Mean 16 mm; SD 4 mm.

questions.explanation: Mean = 80 ÷ 5 = 16 mm. Deviations −2, 0, −1, 2, 1; squares sum to 10. SD = √(10 ÷ 4) = √2.5 = 1.6 mm: the roots typically lie about 1.6 mm from the mean.

questions.stem: A 1999 study found that children who had slept with a light on before the age of two were more likely to become short-sighted later. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on at night, and short sight is partly inherited. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Night-time lighting causes short sight, because the 1999 correlation was found in a large group of children.
The correlation can be explained by parents' short sight, which is linked to both variables.
The 1999 correlation must have been a mistake: the children with night lights were not really more short-sighted.
The later studies prove that light at night has no effect on the eye at all.
